claim: ATAC-seq is a tagmentation-based method whereby Tn5 transposase inserts sequencing adapters into accessible DNA.
source: A popular example is ATAC-seq, whereby Tn5 transposase inserts sequencing adapters into accessible DNA ('tagmentation').
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ATAC-seq method described in the abstract.

claim: CUT&Tag is a tagmentation-based epigenomic profiling method in which antibody tethering of Tn5 to a chromatin epitope profiles specific chromatin features in small samples and single cells.
source: CUT&Tag is a tagmentation-based epigenomic profiling method in which antibody tethering of Tn5 to a chromatin epitope of interest profiles specific chromatin features in small samples and single cells.
evidence: This is a description of the CUT&Tag method from the abstract, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Modifying tagmentation conditions for histone H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 CUT&Tag redirects antibody-tethered tagmentation to accessible DNA sites.
source: Here, we show that by simply modifying the tagmentation conditions for histone H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 CUT&Tag, antibody-tethered tagmentation of accessible DNA sites is redirected to produce chromatin accessibility maps that are indistinguishable from the best ATAC-seq maps.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Modified H3K4me2/H3K4me3 CUT&Tag produces chromatin accessibility maps indistinguishable from the best ATAC-seq maps.
source: Here, we show that by simply modifying the tagmentation conditions for histone H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 CUT&Tag, antibody-tethered tagmentation of accessible DNA sites is redirected to produce chromatin accessibility maps that are indistinguishable from the best ATAC-seq maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: All steps from nuclei to amplified sequencing-ready libraries can be performed in single PCR tubes.
source: Thus, chromatin accessibility maps can be produced in parallel with CUT&Tag maps of other epitopes with all steps from nuclei to amplified sequencing-ready libraries performed in single PCR tubes in the laboratory or on a home workbench.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental protocol described in the methods and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: H3K4 methylation is produced by transcription at promoters and enhancers.
source: As H3K4 methylation is produced by transcription at promoters and enhancers, our method identifies transcription-coupled accessible regulatory sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H3K4 methylation cited in the introduction.

claim: The CUTAC method identifies transcription-coupled accessible regulatory sites.
source: As H3K4 methylation is produced by transcription at promoters and enhancers, our method identifies transcription-coupled accessible regulatory sites.
evidence: This is supported by data showing correspondence with PRO-seq and RNAPII signals in Figure 6.

claim: DNaseI hypersensitivity was first described by Weintraub and Groudine more than 40 years ago.
source: Identification of DNA accessibility in the chromatin landscape has been used to infer active transcription ever since the seminal description of DNaseI hypersensitivity by Weintraub and Groudine more than 40 years ago (Weintraub and Groudine, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original work.

claim: Nucleosomes occupy most of the eukaryotic chromatin landscape.
source: Because nucleosomes occupy most of the eukaryotic chromatin landscape and regulatory elements are mostly free of nucleosomes when they are active, DNA accessibility mapping can potentially identify active regulatory elements genome-wide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chromatin structure.

claim: Regulatory elements are mostly free of nucleosomes when they are active.
source: Because nucleosomes occupy most of the eukaryotic chromatin landscape and regulatory elements are mostly free of nucleosomes when they are active, DNA accessibility mapping can potentially identify active regulatory elements genome-wide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about regulatory element structure.

claim: DNA accessibility mapping can potentially identify active regulatory elements genome-wide.
source: Because nucleosomes occupy most of the eukaryotic chromatin landscape and regulatory elements are mostly free of nucleosomes when they are active, DNA accessibility mapping can potentially identify active regulatory elements genome-wide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between nucleosome depletion and regulatory element activity.

claim: The speed and simplicity of ATAC-seq has led to its widespread adoption.
source: The speed and simplicity of ATAC-seq, in which the cut-and-paste transposition reaction inserts sequencing adapters in the most accessible genomic regions (tagmentation), has led to its widespread adoption in many laboratories for mapping presumed regulatory elements.
evidence: This is a general observation about the field supported by the prevalence of ATAC-seq in the literature.

claim: The median difference between an accessible and a non-accessible site in DNA is only approximately 20%.
source: Furthermore accessibility is not all-or-none, with the median difference between an accessible and a non-accessible site in DNA estimated to be only ~20%, with no sites completely accessible or inaccessible in a population of cells (Chereji et al., 2019; Oberbeckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: No sites are completely accessible or inaccessible in a population of cells.
source: Furthermore accessibility is not all-or-none, with the median difference between an accessible and a non-accessible site in DNA estimated to be only ~20%, with no sites completely accessible or inaccessible in a population of cells (Chereji et al., 2019; Oberbeckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: DNA accessibility mapping strategies show excellent correspondence between methods based on very different strategies.
source: Despite these uncertainties, DNA accessibility mapping has successfully predicted the locations of active gene enhancers and promoters genome-wide, with excellent correspondence between methods based on very different strategies (Karabacak Calviello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comparative study.

claim: Nucleosomes have evolved to repress transcription by blocking sites of pre-initiation complex formation and transcription factor binding.
source: This is likely because DNA accessibility mapping strategies rely on the fact that nucleosomes have evolved to repress transcription by blocking sites of pre-initiation complex formation and transcription factor binding (Kornberg and Lorch, 2020), and so creating and maintaining a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) is a pre-requisite for promoter and enhancer function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established work on nucleosome function.

claim: Creating and maintaining a nucleosome-depleted region is a pre-requisite for promoter and enhancer function.
source: This is likely because DNA accessibility mapping strategies rely on the fact that nucleosomes have evolved to repress transcription by blocking sites of pre-initiation complex formation and transcription factor binding (Kornberg and Lorch, 2020), and so creating and maintaining a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) is a pre-requisite for promoter and enhancer function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the repressive function of nucleosomes.

claim: Enzymes that modify histone tails and chaperones that deposit nucleosome subunits are most active close to sites of transcription initiation.
source: The rationale for this mapping strategy is that the enzymes that modify histone tails and the chaperones that deposit nucleosome subunits are most active close to the sites of initiation of transcription, which typically occurs bidirectionally at both gene promoters and enhancers to produce stable mRNAs and unstable enhancer RNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modification and variant deposition.

claim: Transcription initiation typically occurs bidirectionally at both gene promoters and enhancers.
source: The rationale for this mapping strategy is that the enzymes that modify histone tails and the chaperones that deposit nucleosome subunits are most active close to the sites of initiation of transcription, which typically occurs bidirectionally at both gene promoters and enhancers to produce stable mRNAs and unstable enhancer RNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcription at regulatory elements.

claim: Direct evidence is lacking that a histone mark is associated with an NDR.
source: Although the marks left behind by active transcriptional initiation 'point back' to the NDR, this cause-effect connection between the NDR and the histone marks is only by inference (Wang et al., 2020), and direct evidence is lacking that a histone mark is associated with an NDR.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Reducing ionic concentration during tagmentation preferentially attracts Tn5 tethered to H3K4me2 to the nearby NDR.
source: We provide evidence that reducing the ionic concentration during tagmentation preferentially attracts Tn5 tethered to the H3K4me2 histone modification via a Protein A/G fusion to the nearby NDR, shifting the site of tagmentation from nucleosomes bordering the NDR to the NDR itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Low-salt tagmentation shifts the site of tagmentation from nucleosomes bordering the NDR to the NDR itself.
source: We provide evidence that reducing the ionic concentration during tagmentation preferentially attracts Tn5 tethered to the H3K4me2 histone modification via a Protein A/G fusion to the nearby NDR, shifting the site of tagmentation from nucleosomes bordering the NDR to the NDR itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Almost all transcription-coupled accessible sites correspond to ATAC-seq sites and vice-versa.
source: Almost all transcription-coupled accessible sites correspond to ATAC-seq sites and vice-versa, and lie upstream of paused RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII).
evidence: This is supported by comparative data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: CUTAC sites lie upstream of paused RNA Polymerase II.
source: Almost all transcription-coupled accessible sites correspond to ATAC-seq sites and vice-versa, and lie upstream of paused RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing alignment with RNAPII signals.

claim: CUTAC data quality is similar to or better than the best ATAC-seq datasets.
source: 'CUTAC' (Cleavage Under Targeted Accessible Chromatin) is conveniently performed in parallel with ordinary CUT&Tag, producing accessible site maps from low cell numbers with signal-to-noise as good as or better than the best ATAC-seq datasets.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data quality metrics in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: CUT&Tag-direct eliminates tube transfers so all steps can be performed in a single PCR tube.
source: We have developed a streamlined version of CUT&Tag that eliminates tube transfers, so that all steps can be efficiently performed in a single PCR tube (Kaya-Okur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the protocol and demonstrated in the methods.

claim: CUT&Tag-direct protocol can be performed on a home workbench with minimal equipment.
source: During the COVID-19 pandemic, we adapted this CUT&Tag-direct protocol for implementation with minimal equipment and space requirements that uses no toxic reagents, so that it can be performed conveniently and safely on a home workbench (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental setup shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and data generated at home.

claim: Tapestation profiles of libraries produced at home detected nucleosomal ladders down to 200 cells for H3K27me3.
source: Tapestation profiles of libraries produced at home detected nucleosomal ladders down to 200 cells for H3K27me3 and nucleosomal and subnucleosomal fragments down to 2000 cells for H3K4me3 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the Tapestation gel images in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Tapestation profiles of libraries produced at home detected nucleosomal and subnucleosomal fragments down to 2000 cells for H3K4me3.
source: Tapestation profiles of libraries produced at home detected nucleosomal ladders down to 200 cells for H3K27me3 and nucleosomal and subnucleosomal fragments down to 2000 cells for H3K4me3 (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the Tapestation gel images in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Similar results were obtained for both at-home and in-lab profiles for H3K4me3 and H3K27me3.
source: Similar results were obtained for both at-home and in-lab profiles for both histone modifications (Figure 1C–D) using pA-Tn5 produced in the laboratory, and results using commercial Protein A/Protein G-Tn5 (pAG-Tn5) were at least as good.
evidence: This is shown by comparison of tracks in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Commercial pAG-Tn5 provided results at least as good as lab-produced pA-Tn5.
source: Similar results were obtained for both at-home and in-lab profiles for both histone modifications (Figure 1C–D) using pA-Tn5 produced in the laboratory, and results using commercial Protein A/Protein G-Tn5 (pAG-Tn5) were at least as good.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results using different Tn5 preparations.

claim: Elevated salt conditions are necessary to avoid tagmenting accessible DNA during CUT&Tag.
source: Because the Tn5 domain of pA-Tn5 binds avidly to DNA, it is necessary to use elevated salt conditions to avoid tagmenting accessible DNA during CUT&Tag.
evidence: This is based on understanding of Tn5 DNA-binding properties and experimental observations.

claim: High-salt buffers included 300 mM NaCl for pA-Tn5 binding, washing, and tagmentation at 37°C.
source: High-salt buffers included 300 mM NaCl for pA-Tn5 binding, washing to remove excess protein, and tagmentation at 37°C.
evidence: This describes the standard CUT&Tag protocol conditions.

claim: Protocols without a high-salt wash step result in chromatin profiles dominated by accessible site tagmentation.
source: We have found that other protocols based on the same principle but that do not include a high-salt wash step result in chromatin profiles that are dominated by accessible site tagmentation (Kaya-Okur et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and experimental observations.

claim: Low-salt tagmentation resulted in a marked reduction in the oligo-nucleosome ladder with an increase in faster migrating fragments for H3K4me2.
source: Tapestation capillary gel electrophoresis of the final libraries revealed that after a 20 min incubation the effect of low-salt tagmentation on H3K4me2 CUT&Tag samples was a marked reduction in the oligo-nucleosome ladder with an increase in faster migrating fragments (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly shown in the Tapestation gel images in Figure 3A.

claim: Under low-salt conditions, the broad nucleosomal distribution of H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 CUT&Tag around promoters was mostly replaced by single narrow peaks.
source: Strikingly, under low-salt conditions, high-resolution profiles of H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 showed that the broad nucleosomal distribution of CUT&Tag around promoters for these two modifications was mostly replaced by single narrow peaks (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in the tracks in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Low-salt tagmentation revealed much narrower profiles for H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 (approximately 40% peak width at half-height).
source: In contrast, tagmentation under low-salt conditions revealed much narrower profiles for H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 (~40% peak width at half-height), less so for H3K4me1 (~60%), which suggests that the shift is from H3K4me-marked nucleosomes to an adjacent NDR.
evidence: This is shown in the average plots in Figure 3C.

claim: Low-salt tagmentation revealed less narrowing for H3K4me1 (approximately 60% peak width at half-height).
source: In contrast, tagmentation under low-salt conditions revealed much narrower profiles for H3K4me3 and H3K4me2 (~40% peak width at half-height), less so for H3K4me1 (~60%), which suggests that the shift is from H3K4me-marked nucleosomes to an adjacent NDR.
evidence: This is shown in the average plots in Figure 3C.

claim: Peak narrowing does not require free pAG-Tn5.
source: We also observed a narrowing if we included a stringent 300 mM washing step before low-salt tagmentation (Figure 3D, 'Post-wash'), which indicates that peak narrowing does not require free pAG-Tn5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the post-wash experiment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A small amount of free pAG-Tn5 during tagmentation results in higher yields with increased peak narrowing.
source: However, if a small amount of pAG-Tn5 was included during tagmentation we obtained higher yields with increased peak narrowing (Figure 3D 'Add-back').
evidence: This is shown in the add-back experiment in Figure 3D.

claim: H3K4 methylation is deposited in a gradient of tri- to di- to mono-methylation downstream of the +1 nucleosome from the TSS.
source: As H3K4 methylation is deposited in a gradient of tri- to di- to mono-methylation downstream of the +1 nucleosome from the transcriptional start site (TSS) (Henikoff and Shilatifard, 2011; Soares et al., 2017), we reasoned that the closer proximity of di- and tri-methylated nucleosomes to the NDR than mono-methylated nucleosomes resulted in preferential proximity-dependent 'capture' of Tn5.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on H3K4 methylation patterns.

claim: The shift from broad to more peaky NDR profiles by H3K4me2 low-salt tagmentation was enhanced by addition of 1,6-hexanediol.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we observed that the shift from broad to more peaky NDR profiles and heatmaps by H3K4me2 low-salt tagmentation was enhanced by addition of 1,6-hexanediol, a strongly polar aliphatic alcohol, and by 10% dimethylformamide, a strongly polar amide, both of which enhance chromatin accessibility (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmaps and average plots in Figure 3E-F.

claim: The shift from broad to more peaky NDR profiles by H3K4me2 low-salt tagmentation was enhanced by addition of dimethylformamide.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we observed that the shift from broad to more peaky NDR profiles and heatmaps by H3K4me2 low-salt tagmentation was enhanced by addition of 1,6-hexanediol, a strongly polar aliphatic alcohol, and by 10% dimethylformamide, a strongly polar amide, both of which enhance chromatin accessibility (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmaps and average plots in Figure 3E-F.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol and dimethylformamide enhance chromatin accessibility.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we observed that the shift from broad to more peaky NDR profiles and heatmaps by H3K4me2 low-salt tagmentation was enhanced by addition of 1,6-hexanediol, a strongly polar aliphatic alcohol, and by 10% dimethylformamide, a strongly polar amide, both of which enhance chromatin accessibility (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is stated as a property of these compounds.

claim: NDR-focused tagmentation persisted even in the presence of both strongly polar compounds at 55°C.
source: NDR-focused tagmentation persisted even in the presence of both strongly polar compounds at 55°C.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Localization to NDRs is more precise for small (≤120 bp) than large (>120 bp) tagmented fragments.
source: Localization to NDRs is more precise for small (≤120 bp) than large (>120 bp) tagmented fragments, and by resolving more closely spaced peaks inclusion of these compounds increased the number of peaks called (Figure 3G), also for H3K4me3-tethered Tn5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in the fragment size analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: Inclusion of chromatin-disrupting compounds increased the number of peaks called.
source: Localization to NDRs is more precise for small (≤120 bp) than large (>120 bp) tagmented fragments, and by resolving more closely spaced peaks inclusion of these compounds increased the number of peaks called (Figure 3G), also for H3K4me3-tethered Tn5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Most ATAC-seq sites are flanked by H3K4me2-marked nucleosomes in K562 cells.
source: Using CUT&Tag, we previously showed that most ATAC-seq sites are flanked by H3K4me2-marked nucleosomes in K562 cells (Kaya-Okur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Alignment of ATAC-seq datasets over peaks called using low-salt tagmented CUT&Tag data produced narrow heatmap patterns for the vast majority of peaks.
source: In contrast, alignment of ATAC-seq datasets over peaks called using low-salt tagmented CUT&Tag data produced narrow heatmap patterns for the vast majority of peaks (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmaps in Figure 4B.

claim: Heatmaps produced using either Omni-ATAC or CUTAC peak calls showed occupancy of approximately 95% for ENCODE ATAC-seq data.
source: Remarkably, heatmaps produced using either Omni-ATAC or CUTAC peak calls for the same ENCODE ATAC-seq data showed occupancy of ~95% for both sets of peaks (compare right panels of Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmaps in Figure 4B-C.

claim: There is approximately 50% overlap between ENCODE ATAC-seq peaks and peaks called from either Omni-ATAC or CUTAC data.
source: We found ~50% overlap between ENCODE ATAC-seq peaks and peaks called from either Omni-ATAC (50.0%) or CUTAC (51.3%) data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CUTAC and Omni-ATAC detect the same chromatin features.
source: This equivalence between H3K4me2 CUTAC and Omni-ATAC when compared to ENCODE ATAC-seq implies that CUTAC and Omni-ATAC detect the same chromatin features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data in Figure 4.

claim: H3K4me3 CUTAC shows only approximately 75% peak occupancy with ENCODE ATAC-seq data.
source: This conclusion does not hold for H3K4me3 CUTAC, because similar alignment of ENCODE ATAC-seq data resulted in only ~75% peak occupancy (Figure 4D) and lower correlations (Figure 4E), which we attribute to the greater enrichment of H3K4me3 around promoters than enhancers relative to H3K4me2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: 86% of DNaseI hypersensitive CTCF sites are occupied by CUTAC signal.
source: We observed that 86% of the DNaseI hypersensitive CTCF sites are occupied by CUTAC signal relative to flanking regions (Figure 4F), which suggests equivalence of CUTAC and DNaseI hypersensitive CTCF sites.
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 4F.

claim: H3K4me2 CUT&Tag showed detectable signal at only 53% of DNaseI hypersensitive CTCF sites.
source: We also found that the H3K4me2 CUT&Tag sample showed detectable signal at only 53% of the CTCF sites.
evidence: This is based on analysis of CTCF sites shown in Figure 4F.

claim: For CUT&Tag, FRiP equals approximately 0.4 for 3.2 million fragments.
source: For both ENCODE ChIP-seq and our published CUT&RUN data we measured FRiP = ~0.2 for 3.2 million fragments, whereas for CUT&Tag, FRiP = ~0.4, reflecting improved signal-to-noise relative to previous chromatin profiling methods (Kaya-Okur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on data quality analysis of CUT&Tag data.

claim: H3K4me2 CUT&Tag FRiP equals 0.41 for 3.2 million fragments and approximately 16,000 peaks.
source: Using CUT&Tag-direct, H3K4me2 CUT&Tag FRiP = 0.41 for 3.2 million fragments and ~16,000 peaks (n = 4 replicates), whereas tagmentation by dilution in 2 mM MgCl2 resulted in FRiP = 0.18 for 3.2 million fragments and ~15,000 peaks (n = 4) with similar values for tagmentation by removal [FRiP = 0.21,~15,000 peaks (n = 4)].
evidence: This is based on data quality analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Tagmentation by dilution in 2 mM MgCl2 resulted in FRiP equals 0.18 for 3.2 million fragments and approximately 15,000 peaks.
source: Using CUT&Tag-direct, H3K4me2 CUT&Tag FRiP = 0.41 for 3.2 million fragments and ~16,000 peaks (n = 4 replicates), whereas tagmentation by dilution in 2 mM MgCl2 resulted in FRiP = 0.18 for 3.2 million fragments and ~15,000 peaks (n = 4) with similar values for tagmentation by removal [FRiP = 0.21,~15,000 peaks (n = 4)].
evidence: This is based on data quality analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: CUTAC data quality was similar to that for the Omni-ATAC method.
source: We also compared the number of peaks and FRiP values for CUTAC to those for ATAC-seq for K562 cells and observed that CUTAC data quality was similar to that for the Omni-ATAC method (Corces et al., 2017), better than ENCODE ATAC-seq (Zhang et al., 2020), and much better than Fast-ATAC (Corces et al., 2016), a previous improvement over Standard ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the comparative analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: CUTAC is relatively insensitive to tagmentation times.
source: CUTAC is relatively insensitive to tagmentation times, with similar numbers of peaks and similar FRiP values for samples tagmented for 5, 20 and 60 min (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A comparing different tagmentation times.

claim: The robustness of CUT&Tag and CUTAC is attributed to the tethering of Tn5 to specific chromatin epitopes.
source: We attribute the robustness of CUT&Tag and CUTAC to the tethering of Tn5 to specific chromatin epitopes, so that when tagmentation goes to completion there is little untethered Tn5 that would increase background levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of the method.

claim: ATAC-seq data from multiple laboratories shows a wide range of data quality.
source: When we measured peak numbers and FRiP values for ATAC-seq for K562 data deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) from multiple laboratories, we observed a wide range of data quality (Figure 5B, even from very recent submissions from expert groups: Table 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Table 1.

claim: Variability in ATAC-seq data quality is attributed to difficulty avoiding background tagmentation by excess free Tn5.
source: We attribute this variability to the difficulty of avoiding background tagmention by excess free Tn5 in ATAC-seq protocols and subsequent release of non-specific nucleosomal fragments (Swanson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of the ATAC-seq method, supported by citation.

claim: Excluding larger fragments results in better resolution yielding more peaks and higher FRiP values.
source: Indeed this is exactly what we observe for heatmaps (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), tracks (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), peak calls and FRiP values (Figure 5C). Excluding larger fragments results in better resolution yielding more peaks and higher FRIP values, both of which approach a maximum with fewer fragments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Addition of strongly polar compounds during tagmentation provides substantial improvement in peak calling and FRiPs.
source: Moreover, the addition of strongly polar compounds during tagmentation provides a substantial improvement in peak calling and FRiPs (Figure 5C, turquoise and orange curves).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Excluding large fragments did not improve ATAC-seq peak calls and FRiP values.
source: Excluding large fragments did not improve ATAC-seq peak calls and FRiP values, which indicates that tethering to H3K4me2 is critical for maximum sensitivity and resolution of DNA accessibility maps.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Tethering to H3K4me2 is critical for maximum sensitivity and resolution of DNA accessibility maps.
source: Excluding large fragments did not improve ATAC-seq peak calls and FRiP values, which indicates that tethering to H3K4me2 is critical for maximum sensitivity and resolution of DNA accessibility maps.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data in Figure 5C.

claim: H3K4me2/3 methylation marks active transcription at promoters.
source: H3K4me2/3 methylation marks active transcription at promoters (Gilchrist et al., 2012), which raises the question as to whether sites identified by CUTAC are also sites of RNAPII enrichment genome-wide.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CUTAC peaks are located in the NDR between flanking H3K4me2-marked chromatin.
source: CUT&Tag H3K4me2 peaks flank NDRs more downstream on either side than H3K4me3, confirmed by ENCODE ChIP-seq data to be the actual location of these marks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). In contrast, CUTAC peaks are located in the NDR between flanking H3K4me2-marked chromatin (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CUTAC sites at promoter NDRs correspond closely to promoter ATAC-seq sites.
source: CUTAC sites at promoter NDRs corresponded closely to promoter ATAC-seq sites, consistent with expectation for promoter NDRs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Paired CUT&Tag and CUTAC samples can replace both ChIP-seq for an active promoter mark and ATAC-seq in a single experiment.
source: Thus, paired CUT&Tag and CUTAC samples can replace both ChIP-seq for an active promoter mark and ATAC-seq in a single experiment with identical processing, analysis and display.
evidence: This is an inference based on the equivalence of CUTAC to ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag to ChIP-seq.

claim: About 80% of CUTAC sites showed enrichment of PRO-Seq signal downstream.
source: About 80% of the CUTAC sites showed enrichment of PRO-Seq signal downstream, confirming that the large majority of CUTAC sites correspond to NDRs representing transcription-coupled regulatory elements.
evidence: This is based on analysis of PRO-seq data aligned to CUTAC peaks in Figure 6C.

claim: The large majority of CUTAC sites correspond to NDRs representing transcription-coupled regulatory elements.
source: About 80% of the CUTAC sites showed enrichment of PRO-Seq signal downstream, confirming that the large majority of CUTAC sites correspond to NDRs representing transcription-coupled regulatory elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PRO-seq enrichment data.

claim: There is only a approximately 20% median difference in absolute DNA accessibility between DNaseI hypersensitive sites and non-hypersensitive sites genome-wide.
source: In part this uncertainty is attributable to variations in nucleosome positioning within a population of mammalian cells such that there is only a ~20% median difference in absolute DNA accessibility between DNaseI hypersensitive sites and non-hypersensitive sites genome-wide (Chereji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: DNA accessibility is not the primary determinant of gene regulation.
source: This suggests that DNA accessibility is not the primary determinant of gene regulation, and contradicts the popular characterization of accessible DNA sites as 'open' and the lack of accessibility as 'closed'.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small difference in accessibility between sites.

claim: There are multiple dynamic processes that can result in nucleosome depletion, including transcription, nucleosome remodeling, transcription factor binding, and replication.
source: Moreover, there are multiple dynamic processes that can result in nucleosome depletion, including transcription, nucleosome remodeling, transcription factor binding, and replication, so that the identification of a presumed regulatory element by chromatin accessibility mapping leaves open the question as to how accessibility is established and maintained.
evidence: This is general knowledge about chromatin dynamics.

claim: CUTAC provides a physical link between a transcription-coupled process and DNA hyperaccessibility.
source: Our CUTAC mapping method now provides a physical link between a transcription-coupled process and DNA hyperaccessibility by showing that anchoring of Tn5 to a nucleosome mark laid down by transcriptional events immediately downstream identifies presumed gene regulatory elements that are indistinguishable from those identified by ATAC-seq.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: The equivalence of CUTAC and ATAC at both enhancers and promoters provides support for the hypothesis that these regulatory elements are characterized by the same regulatory architecture.
source: The equivalence of CUTAC and ATAC at both enhancers and promoters provides support for the hypothesis that these regulatory elements are characterized by the same regulatory architecture (Andersson et al., 2015; Arnold et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data, supported by citations to prior hypotheses.

claim: H3K4 methylation is catalyzed by COMPASS/SET1 and related enzyme complexes in all eukaryotes.
source: In all eukaryotes, H3K4 methylation is catalyzed by COMPASS/SET1 and related enzyme complexes, which associate with the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the large subunit of RNAPII when Serine-5 of the tandemly repetitive heptad repeat of the CTD is phosphorylated following transcription initiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H3K4 methylation, supported by citations.

claim: COMPASS/SET1 complexes associate with the CTD of RNAPII when Serine-5 is phosphorylated following transcription initiation.
source: In all eukaryotes, H3K4 methylation is catalyzed by COMPASS/SET1 and related enzyme complexes, which associate with the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the large subunit of RNAPII when Serine-5 of the tandemly repetitive heptad repeat of the CTD is phosphorylated following transcription initiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of H3K4 methylation.

claim: The enrichment of dimethylated and trimethylated forms of H3K4 is thought to be the result of exposure of the H3 tail to COMPASS/SET1 during RNAPII stalling just downstream of the TSS.
source: The enrichment of dimethylated and trimethylated forms of H3K4 is thought to be the result of exposure of the H3 tail to COMPASS/SET1 during RNAPII stalling just downstream of the TSS, so that these modifications are coupled to the onset of transcription (Soares et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Tn5 tethered to H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 efficiently tagments accessible sites.
source: Therefore, our demonstration that Tn5 tethered to H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 histone tail residues efficiently tagments accessible sites, implies that accessibility at regulatory elements is created by events immediately following transcription initiation.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing CUTAC detects accessible sites.

claim: Accessibility at regulatory elements is created by events immediately following transcription initiation.
source: Therefore, our demonstration that Tn5 tethered to H3K4me2 or H3K4me3 histone tail residues efficiently tagments accessible sites, implies that accessibility at regulatory elements is created by events immediately following transcription initiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coupling of H3K4 methylation to transcription initiation and the CUTAC results.

claim: This mechanistic interpretation is supported by the mapping of CUTAC sites just upstream of RNAPII.
source: This mechanistic interpretation is supported by the mapping of CUTAC sites just upstream of RNAPII, and is consistent with the recent demonstration that PRO-seq data can be used to accurately impute 'active' histone modifications (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the alignment data in Figure 6 showing CUTAC sites upstream of RNAPII.

claim: Approximately 95% of ATAC-seq peaks are detected by CUTAC and vice-versa.
source: Thus CUTAC identifies active promoters and enhancers that produce enhancer RNAs, which might help explain why ~95% of ATAC-seq peaks are detected by CUTAC and vice-versa (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is based on the overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: All steps from frozen nuclei to purified sequencing-ready libraries can be performed in a day in single PCR tubes on a home workbench.
source: Like CUT&Tag-direct, all steps from frozen nuclei to purified sequencing-ready libraries for the data presented here were performed in a day in single PCR tubes on a home workbench.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental setup and results presented.

claim: CUTAC can be performed in parallel with an H3K4me2 CUT&Tag positive control and other antibodies using multiple aliquots from each population of cells.
source: As it requires only a simple modification of one step in the CUT&Tag protocol, CUTAC can be performed in parallel with an H3K4me2 CUT&Tag positive control and other antibodies using multiple aliquots from each population of cells to be profiled.
evidence: This is based on the protocol design and demonstrated in the experiments.

claim: Three distinct protocol modifications (dilution, removal and post-wash tagmentation) yield high-quality results.
source: We have shown that three distinct protocol modifications, dilution, removal and post-wash tagmentation yield high-quality results, providing flexibility that might be important for adapting CUTAC to nuclei from diverse cell types and tissues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative data in Figure 3.

claim: CUT&Tag is highly reproducible using native or lightly cross-linked cells or nuclei.
source: In contrast, CUT&Tag is highly reproducible using native or lightly cross-linked cells or nuclei (Kaya-Okur et al., 2020), and as shown here H3K4me2 CUTAC maps regulatory elements with sensitivity and signal-to-noise comparable to the best ATAC-seq datasets, even better when larger fragments are computationally excluded.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data in this study.

claim: H3K4me2 CUTAC maps regulatory elements with sensitivity and signal-to-noise comparable to the best ATAC-seq datasets.
source: In contrast, CUT&Tag is highly reproducible using native or lightly cross-linked cells or nuclei (Kaya-Okur et al., 2020), and as shown here H3K4me2 CUTAC maps regulatory elements with sensitivity and signal-to-noise comparable to the best ATAC-seq datasets, even better when larger fragments are computationally excluded.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative data quality analysis in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The combination of H3K4me2 CUT&Tag and CUTAC provides both highest data quality and precise mapping using the same H3K4me2 antibody.
source: Although datasets from H3K4me2 CUT&Tag have lower background than datasets from CUTAC run in parallel, the combination of the two provides both highest data quality (CUT&Tag) and precise mapping (CUTAC) using the same H3K4me2 antibody.
evidence: This is based on the comparative analysis of CUT&Tag and CUTAC data.
